---
title: "RBIG — Rotation-Based Iterative Gaussianization"
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd() / "src"))
from lectures import plotting, datasets
from lectures.plotting import INK, COOL, WARM, CRASH, despine, annotate_box
from lectures.gaussianization import gaussianize_1d
from rbig import AnnealedRBIG
from lectures.measures import cocrash_fraction
plotting.set_style("notes")
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.gridspec import GridSpec


def jointplot(fig, spec, data, color, title="", s=6, lim=None, equal=False, overlay=None):
    """Scatter with top/right marginal histograms, drawn inside one GridSpec cell.

    Showing the marginals beside the joint is the whole point: it lets the reader
    see Gaussian marginals sitting on top of a non-Gaussian joint, marginals
    skewing after a rotation, and marginals re-flattening after Gaussianization.
    """
    sub = spec.subgridspec(2, 2, width_ratios=[5, 1.2], height_ratios=[1.2, 5],
                           wspace=0.05, hspace=0.05)
    axm = fig.add_subplot(sub[1, 0])
    axt = fig.add_subplot(sub[0, 0], sharex=axm)
    axr = fig.add_subplot(sub[1, 1], sharey=axm)
    axm.scatter(data[:, 0], data[:, 1], s=s, c=color, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none")
    if overlay is not None:
        overlay(axm)
    axt.hist(data[:, 0], bins=42, color=color, alpha=0.8)
    axr.hist(data[:, 1], bins=42, orientation="horizontal", color=color, alpha=0.8)
    if lim is not None:
        axm.set_xlim(*lim); axm.set_ylim(*lim)
    if equal:
        axm.set_aspect("equal")
    axm.set_xticks([]); axm.set_yticks([]); despine(axm)
    for a in (axt, axr):
        a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
        for sp in a.spines.values():
            sp.set_visible(False)
    axt.set_title(title, fontsize=11)
    return axm
```

The 1-D [rank → Gaussian](01-change-of-variables.qmd) trick fixes one marginal at
a time but cannot touch the dependence *between* variables.  RBIG fixes that with
one more idea: after Gaussianizing the marginals, **rotate**, so dependence hiding
between coordinates is exposed to the next round of marginal Gaussianization.
Iterate, and the joint converges to a spherical Gaussian.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## One Layer = Two Invertible Steps

$$
x \;\xrightarrow{\;\text{marginal Gaussianize}\;}\; g
\;\xrightarrow{\;\text{rotate } R\;}\; x'
$$

- **Marginal Gaussianize**: $g_j = \Phi^{-1}(\hat F_j(x_j))$ on each coordinate.
- **Rotate**: $x' = g R$ with an orthogonal $R$ (PCA or random).

Both steps are invertible, so the whole stack is.  Each layer's Jacobian is cheap
(a diagonal marginal map times an orthogonal rotation), which is why RBIG scales.
:::

## Why Gaussian Marginals Aren't Enough

It is tempting to think we are done after the [1-D move](01-change-of-variables.qmd):
push every coordinate through $\Phi^{-1}(\hat F_j)$ and each axis becomes a textbook
standard normal.  But a per-axis map is a *monotone reshuffling of one coordinate
at a time* — it slides points along their own axis without ever asking where they
sit on the other.  It **cannot change which** $x_1$ **goes with which** $x_2$.  All
the dependence — the joint geometry — survives untouched.

The cleanest way to see it is a **V**: a curved relationship where $y$ is small at
both extremes of $x$ and large in the middle (a long–straddle payoff is exactly
this shape).  Gaussianize both axes and watch the marginals *vs.* the joint.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rbig-marginals-not-enough
#| fig-cap: "Both marginals are forced to standard normals (the side histograms are textbook bells), yet the joint is still a V. Dependence lives *between* the axes, where a per-coordinate map cannot reach."
u, v = datasets.convex_payoff(n=1500, seed=0)
XV = np.column_stack([u, v])
XV = (XV - XV.mean(0)) / XV.std(0)          # standardize so the "before" is fair
GV = np.column_stack([gaussianize_1d(XV[:, 0]), gaussianize_1d(XV[:, 1])])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.6, 4.4))
gs = GridSpec(1, 2, figure=fig, wspace=0.3)
jointplot(fig, gs[0, 0], XV, COOL, "data: a V", s=7)
jointplot(fig, gs[0, 1], GV, COOL, "both marginals → Gaussian", s=7)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read the right panel carefully.  The **top and right histograms are perfect bells**
— each marginal is now exactly $\mathcal N(0,1)$.  And yet the **scatter is still a
V**.  A test that only looks at one variable at a time would declare victory; the
joint says the variables are as dependent as ever.  Gaussian marginals are
*necessary* for a standard-normal joint, but nowhere near *sufficient*.

This is the gap RBIG closes.  Marginals alone are a dead end — we need a move that
reaches *between* the axes.  That move is a **rotation**.

## Rotate, Re-Gaussianize, Repeat

Here is the trick.  A rotation **mixes the coordinates**: each new axis is a blend
of the old ones.  Leftover dependence that was hiding *between* the axes is dragged
back *onto* the axes, where it resurfaces as **non-Gaussian marginals** — which the
1-D move can then flatten again.  Alternate the two steps and each round scrapes off
a little more dependence:

$$
\underbrace{x \;\xrightarrow{\;\Phi^{-1}(\hat F)\;}\; g}_{\text{marginals} \to \text{Gaussian}}
\;\xrightarrow{\;\text{rotate } R\;}\;
\underbrace{x' \;\xrightarrow{\;\Phi^{-1}(\hat F)\;}\; \cdots}_{\text{repeat}}
$$

Watch one full turn of the loop on the same V.  The marginal histograms are the tell
at every stage:

```{python}
#| label: fig-rbig-loop
#| fig-cap: "One turn of the RBIG loop. (1) Marginals Gaussian but joint still a V. (2) Rotate 45° — the V tips, and the marginals *skew* (the rotation has exposed dependence onto the axes). (3) Re-Gaussianize — marginals flat again, joint a little rounder. (4) Many such turns drive the cloud to a sphere."
def gm(D):
    return np.column_stack([gaussianize_1d(D[:, 0]), gaussianize_1d(D[:, 1])])

def rot(D, deg):
    th = np.deg2rad(deg)
    R = np.array([[np.cos(th), -np.sin(th)], [np.sin(th), np.cos(th)]])
    return D @ R.T

R1 = rot(GV, 45)        # one rotation
G2 = gm(R1)             # re-gaussianize the rotated marginals
ZV = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, random_state=0).fit(XV).transform(XV)

seq = [("marginals Gaussian\n(still a V)", GV),
       ("rotate 45°\n→ marginals skew", R1),
       ("re-Gaussianize\nmarginals", G2),
       ("…repeat → spherical", ZV)]
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 3.6))
gs = GridSpec(1, 4, figure=fig, wspace=0.4)
for i, (t, D) in enumerate(seq):
    jointplot(fig, gs[0, i], D, COOL, t, s=5)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Trace the marginals across the panels: flat → **skewed** → flat again.  The skew in
panel 2 is dependence that the rotation *uncovered*; panel 3 flattens it; the joint
is rounder than where we started.  Run enough turns and the cloud becomes a featureless
sphere — **that alternation, not the marginal step alone, is RBIG.**

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why Aim at a Gaussian (and Not Some Other Target)?

The rotation step is the reason the target *must* be a Gaussian.  A rotation of
**independent Gaussians is still independent Gaussians** — the standard normal is the
only product distribution a rotation leaves alone.  So once the cloud is spherical,
rotating it cannot manufacture new dependence, and the loop has a fixed point to
converge to.  Aim at a uniform or a Laplace and a rotation would re-introduce
dependence on every turn; the loop would never settle.
:::

## One Layer, in Pictures

The two halves of a single layer, shown on a correlated, fat-tailed pair so you can
see the marginals being flattened *and* the joint being decorrelated:

```{python}
#| label: fig-rbig-step
#| fig-cap: "One RBIG layer on a correlated, fat-tailed pair: Gaussianize each marginal (the side histograms become bells), then rotate to decorrelate (the cloud straightens up)."
a, b = datasets.tail_dependent_pair(n=1500, seed=1)
X = np.column_stack([a, b])

G = np.column_stack([gaussianize_1d(X[:, 0]), gaussianize_1d(X[:, 1])])
cov = np.cov(G, rowvar=False)
_, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov)        # PCA rotation
Xr = G @ vecs

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 4.2))
gs = GridSpec(1, 3, figure=fig, wspace=0.3)
panels = [(X, "data (correlated, fat tails)"),
          (G, "after marginal Gaussianize"),
          (Xr, "after rotation (decorrelated)")]
for i, (data, title) in enumerate(panels):
    jointplot(fig, gs[0, i], data, COOL, title, s=7)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Forward to Gaussian, Backward to Data

Stack ~30 layers and the joint *is* a standard Gaussian.  Then run the stack
backward — draw $z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$ and invert each layer — and you generate
fresh samples that keep the **real joint tail**.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rbig-forward-backward
#| fig-cap: "Left: the data. Middle: RBIG forward — a spherical Gaussian. Right: samples drawn backward keep the co-crash (the tail dependence is regenerated, not assumed)."
rbig = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, random_state=0).fit(X)
Z = rbig.transform(X)
gen = rbig.sample(len(X))

cc_data = cocrash_fraction(X[:, 0], X[:, 1])
cc_gen = cocrash_fraction(gen[:, 0], gen[:, 1])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 4.4))
gs = GridSpec(1, 3, figure=fig, wspace=0.32)
panels = [
    (X, COOL, f"data · co-crash {cc_data:.0%}"),
    (Z, plotting.PALETTE["green"], f"RBIG forward · |corr|={abs(np.corrcoef(Z[:,0],Z[:,1])[0,1]):.2f}"),
    (gen, WARM, f"RBIG sample · co-crash {cc_gen:.0%}"),
]
for i, (data, col, title) in enumerate(panels):
    jointplot(fig, gs[0, i], data, col, title, s=7)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The middle panel is round and uncorrelated — the dependence is gone.  The right
panel has it back: **what RBIG removes going forward, it regenerates going
backward.**

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Reading
The forward pass is a dependence *detector* (how hard did we have to work to
Gaussianize?); the backward pass is a dependence *generator*.  The next page
turns the first into a number — [mutual information](03-mutual-information.qmd) —
and [Uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd) leans on the second.
:::
